::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Objective.
It remains unclear which architecture best sorts 12-lead electrocardiograms into diagnostic superclasses, and whether added model complexity pays off.
Methods.

Using 21,375 PTB-XL records under one patient-level split, we compared a Mamba-style state space model, a residual convolutional network, a bidirectional long short-term memory network, a convolutionalrecurrent network with attention, soft-voting ensembles of these networks, and MiniRocket features with LightGBM.
Each record took the superclass of its highest-likelihood diagnostic code, and we scored saved predictions with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals.
Results.
No model clearly outperformed MiniRocket with LightGBM, which needs no graphics processor.

The ensemble of the three deep models with the highest validation macro F1 score reached 0.656, against 0.645 for MiniRocket with LightGBM (difference +0.011, 95% confidence interval -0.007 to +0.031), and an ensemble of all four deep models reached 0.657.

An exploratory ensemble, whose members we chose after seeing test results, reached 0.665 and was the only ensemble whose interval excluded zero (+0.021, 0.002 to 0.040); we regard that margin as optimistic.
Hypertrophy was the hardest class (F1 0.33-0.41), and differences in its recall mostly reflected threshold placement.
Conclusions.
Under one shared split, deep ensembles added little over a classical pipeline.
Significance.
These results give biomedical informatics researchers a statistically grounded reference for judging whether complex models justify their cost on this benchmark.
With one dataset, one split, one training seed per model, and no external validation, they do not show readiness for clinical use.
Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death worldwide [1], and the 12-lead ECG is one of the most widely available ways to detect it.

text.text: Software that reads ECGs already exists, but assigning a recording to a diagnostic category is still hard.
The abnormalities can be subtle, several conditions often appear in the same patient, and the categories are heavily imbalanced.
Deep learning has even found signals that clinicians cannot read from the tracing, such as atrial fibrillation in ECGs recorded during sinus rhythm [2].

text.text: In this paper we compare deep learning and classical approaches on one task.
The task is to assign each 12-lead recording in the public PTB-XL dataset to one of five diagnostic superclasses.

These are conduction disturbance (CD), hypertrophy (HYP, which in PTB-XL covers left and right ventricular hypertrophy, atrial overload or enlargement, and septal hypertrophy), myocardial infarction (MI), normal ECG (NORM), and ST/T change (STTC).
Convolutional networks have generally done well on this kind of task, and recurrent models suit the sequential nature of the signal.
Selective state space models (SSMs) are a newer option for long sequences, and MiniRocket, a random convolutional feature transform, offers an alternative that does not use deep learning.

The six approaches are a Mamba-style SSM (M1), a 1D residual CNN (M2), a BiLSTM (M3), a CRNN with attention (M4), a soft-voting ensemble of M1, M3, and M4 (M5), and a MiniRocket plus LightGBM pipeline (M6).
M5 combines the three deep models with the highest validation macro F1.
We also report two other ensembles as extra checks.
One averages all four deep models (M5A).
The other is an exploratory ensemble of M2, M3, and M4 (M5T), whose members we chose after seeing test results.
Every model with learnable parameters was trained from scratch, and all models were tested on the same 3,182 records, which share no patients with the training or validation data.
Besides argmax macro F1, we report AUROC, AUPRC, per-class results, and calibration, and we compare pairs of models with paired, patient-level statistics.
Our main finding is that no model was clearly better than MiniRocket+LightGBM.
The ensemble chosen on validation was ahead of the Mamba-style SSM and the CRNN, but it was not detectably different from the ResNet, the BiLSTM, or MiniRocket+LightGBM.
Only the test-selected ensemble M5T had an interval over MiniRocket+LightGBM that excluded zero, and that margin is probably optimistic.

text.text: The SCP-ECG diagnostic codes on each recording map to five superclasses (CD, HYP, MI, NORM, STTC).
Records whose codes mapped to no superclass were dropped, which left 21,375 recordings from 18,610 patients.
NORM makes up about 43% of these records, and HYP about 6%.
NORM is the normal-ECG superclass in PTB-XL, not a rhythm category.
Sinus rhythm alone does not make an ECG NORM, and a record with both NORM and an abnormal code takes whichever has the higher likelihood under the rule below.
HYP labels come from ECG criteria, not echocardiography, so HYP is not limited to left ventricular hypertrophy.
Rhythm is a separate statement category in PTB-XL and was not used here, so HYP records were not restricted to non-sinus rhythm.
No IRB approval was needed because the dataset is public, de-identified, and released under a Creative Commons license.

PTB-XL was curated by the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt in Germany from recordings made with Schiller devices between 1989 and 1996, and it covers about 18,900 patients (roughly half women, ages 0 to 95, median about 62) [5].

text.text: Ethnicity is not recorded.
Voltage criteria for hypertrophy differ by age, sex, and ethnic origin, and our labels come from the dataset's annotations, so our results may not carry over to other populations.
Label assignment.
About a quarter of the records (23.7%) carry more than one superclass, so we had to reduce each of them to a single label.
We used the superclass of the highestlikelihood SCP code among codes with likelihood above zero, and we broke ties in favor of the first-listed code.
For 3,130 records (14.6%) the label would change if ties went to the lastlisted code.
The ground truth therefore depends partly on this rule, and the per-class results carry that caveat.
A single label is also a clinical limitation, because several cardiac conditions often occur together in real patients.
Under our tie-breaking rule, a model is penalized in evaluation even when it correctly detects a secondary condition.
This probably understates the multi-label diagnostic ability of both the deep ensembles and the classical pipeline.
No record was excluded for carrying several superclasses, and only records with no superclass code were dropped.

Our F1 scores therefore measure agreement with the dominantcode label, not full ECG interpretation, and we did not measure how performance differs between records with one superclass and records with several.
We did not keep the original label array, so we re-derived the labels from the released metadata.

The test class counts (497, 208, 597, 1,386, and 494 for CD, HYP, MI, NORM, and STTC) fall within two records per class of those from our initial analysis, and each deep model's test macro F1 reproduced to within 0.0011.
Each recording went through three preprocessing steps in order.
A zero-phase IIR notch filter at 50 Hz (Q = 30) removed powerline interference, a reasonable choice for PTB-XL's European recording setting.
A zero-phase fourthorder Butterworth bandpass filter (0.5-40 Hz) removed baseline wander and high-frequency noise.
Both filters used sosfiltfilt, so they add no phase distortion.

Finally, we z-scored each lead in each recording separately, using its own mean and standard deviation within the recording, with a floor of 10 -6 on the standard deviation to avoid division by zero on flat or disconnected leads.
Z-scoring each lead removes absolute voltage and the am-plitude relationships between leads that the voltage criteria for hypertrophy depend on.
The 0.5-40 Hz band also reduces QRS amplitude compared with the 150 Hz diagnostic bandwidth.
Weak HYP performance may therefore reflect our preprocessing as well as class imbalance.
We did not test other normalization or bandwidth settings.
The pipeline ran during signal extraction, so the stored array X of shape (21, 375, 12, 5000) holds only preprocessed float32 signals.

text.text: We split by patient, roughly 70/15/15 into training, validation, and test sets, because a record-level split could put one patient's several recordings on both sides.
We shuffled the 18,610 patient IDs with seed 42 and divided them into disjoint groups of 13,028 training, 2,791 validation, and 2,791 test patients, giving 14,978, 3,215, and 3,182 records.
The split is not stratified by class, and it differs from the recommended PTB-XL strat_fold partition (which also respects patient boundaries).
Our absolute numbers are therefore not directly comparable with published benchmarks.
The comparisons in this paper are relative, among models trained and tested under one shared split.
All models share this split.
For the deep models M1 to M4 we used two mechanisms.
A WeightedRandomSampler weighted each training sample by the inverse of its class frequency, which oversamples minority classes within batches.
We also replaced cross-entropy with focal loss [21] (γ = 1.0, no per-class α weights) and label smoothing of ϵ = 0.1.
text.formatted: We also replaced cross-entropy with focal loss <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> (γ = 1.0, no per-class α weights) and label smoothing of ϵ = 0.1.

text.text: The focal term (1-p t ) γ shifts the gradient toward hard and rare examples, and label smoothing softens the one-hot targets, which suits PTB-XL's likelihoodbased labels.

Stacking all three mechanisms (the sampler, inverse-frequency α weighting, and focal loss with γ = 2.0) overcorrected in early development experiments and gave up too much NORM performance for HYP recall.
So we dropped the α weighting and lowered γ to 1.0.
Those runs were not kept.
We trained M6 without SMOTE [22], a choice made on validation macro F1 (0.649 without, 0.645 with), and used class_weight="balanced" in LightGBM.
text.formatted: We trained M6 without SMOTE <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>, a choice made on validation macro F1 (0.649 without, 0.645 with), and used class_weight="balanced" in LightGBM.

text.text: The SMOTE variant, which expands the training set from 14,978 to 32,190 samples, is reported as an ablation.
We augmented the training data for M1 to M4 with six transforms, each applied independently with a fixed probability.
Gaussian noise had a standard deviation of 1% of the signal's own (probability 0.5).
Amplitude scaling ranged from 0.9 to 1.1 (0.3), and a circular time shift reached up to ±50 samples (0.3).
One random lead was zeroed (0.15) so the model could not rely on any single lead.
Simulated baseline wander, a sinusoidal drift with frequency between 0.05 and 0.5 Hz and amplitude between 0.05 and 0.15 (0.4), mimicked breathing and motion artifacts.
Finally, the six limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) were randomly permuted with probability 0.2 to reduce sensitivity to lead order.
The limb-lead permutation is a problem for some labels.
It changes the frontal-plane axis and moves findings such as inferior Q waves into other leads, which can change the meaning of an MI or axis-dependent conduction label.
We did not run an ablation, so it may have hurt M1 to M4 on those classes.
C. Model Architectures M1 (Mamba-style SSM, pure PyTorch).
This is a selective state space model inspired by Mamba [11], written entirely in PyTorch with no custom CUDA kernels.
text.formatted: This is a selective state space model inspired by Mamba <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, written entirely in PyTorch with no custom CUDA kernels.

text.text: A two-stage convolutional stem (strides 4 and 4) cuts the 5,000-sample input to 313 time steps with d model = 128 channels.
Four MambaBlock modules follow the stem.
Each block applies layer normalization, an input projection to 2 × d inner = 512 channels, a depthwise Conv1d with kernel size 4, a SiLU activation, and a selective scan with d state = 16.
We compute the scan in parallel, not as a sequential recurrence, using a prefix sum over log-space cumulative products of the discretized state transition matrices.
Mean and max pooling over the 313 output steps give a 256-dimensional vector, which feeds a two-layer head with GELU activations and dropout of 0.2.
The model has about 1.1 million parameters and was trained with a learning rate of 2 × 10 -4 and batch size 32.
This ResNet-style network [8] works directly on the raw 12-lead signal of shape (12, 5000).
text.formatted: This ResNet-style network <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> works directly on the raw 12-lead signal of shape <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12,</ref> <ref type="bibr">5000)</ref>.

text.text: A stem with kernel size 15, stride 2, and max pooling feeds four residual stages with 64, 128, 256, and 512 channels, each made of two ResidualBlock1D modules (kernel size 7, batch normalization, ReLU, dropout 0.2).
Adaptive average pooling then reduces the time axis to a single step.
A twolayer head with dropout 0.3 produces the five outputs.
It has about 8.9 million parameters and was trained with a learning rate of 3 × 10 -4 and batch size 64.
A bidirectional LSTM [10] runs on a convolutional summary of the raw signal.
text.formatted: A bidirectional LSTM <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> runs on a convolutional summary of the raw signal.

text.text: A three-stage stem with strides 4, 2, and 2 shortens the sequence from 5,000 to about 313 steps and projects to 96 channels.
A two-layer bidirectional LSTM (hidden size 192, dropout 0.3) follows.
Mean and max pooling over time give a 768-dimensional vector for a two-layer head.
The model has about 1.5 million parameters; training used a learning rate of 5×10 -4 and batch size 64.
A three-stage 1D convolutional extractor (kernel sizes 11, 7, and 5; strides 2, 2, and 2) produces 128 channels.
A two-layer bidirectional LSTM (hidden size 256, dropout 0.3) and temporal attention come next.
Attention weights come from a learned linear projection of the 512-dimensional LSTM output to a scalar, normalized by a softmax over time.
The weighted sum is the final sequence representation.
The model has about 2.6 million parameters; training used a learning rate of 4 × 10 -4 and batch size 64.
M5 (soft-voting ensemble of M1, M3, and M4, selected on validation).
M5 averages the softmax outputs of M1, M3, and M4 and needed no further training.
Its members are the three deep models with the highest validation macro F1 (M4, M1, M3), so the selection rule uses no test information.
The order of events matters here.
Our first ensemble was M2+M3+M4, whose members we picked using test macro F1.
We adopted the validation-based rule as the main definition only after seeing that result.
We therefore report two more ensembles next to M5.
M5A averages all four deep models and involves no selection.
M5T is the original M2+M3+M4 ensemble.
Because test results guided its choice, we treat it as exploratory and expect its advantage to be optimistic.
M6 is not a neural network and serves as a separate classical baseline.
We applied the MiniRocketMultivariate transform from sktime [16] with 10,000 random convolutional kernels, which produces a 9,996-dimensional vector of proportions of positive values per recording.
text.formatted: We applied the MiniRocketMultivariate transform from sktime <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> with 10,000 random convolutional kernels, which produces a 9,996-dimensional vector of proportions of positive values per recording.

text.text: We fit the transform on a random 5,000-record subset of the training set only.
The kernel weights do not depend on labels, but the bias values are set from the data, so fitting on training records alone keeps validation and test signals out of the transform.
We then extracted features for all records in chunks of 1,000 and standardized them with a scaler fit on the training set.
LightGBM [17] used at most 400 trees, num_leaves = 31, learning_rate = 0.05, colsample_bytree = 0.3, subsample = 0.8, and class_weight="balanced".
text.formatted: LightGBM <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> used at most 400 trees, num_leaves = 31, learning_rate = 0.05, colsample_bytree = 0.3, subsample = 0.8, and class_weight="balanced".

text.text: Early stopping with patience 50 on the validation set chose the number of trees (221 without SMOTE, 196 with).
The remaining hyperparameters were fixed in advance and not tuned.

We trained M1 to M4 with AdamW [23] (weight decay 10 -4 ) and a cosine annealing schedule over at most 70 epochs, with early stopping (patience 12) on validation macro F1 and gradient clipping at a maximum norm of 1.0.
text.formatted: We trained M1 to M4 with AdamW <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> (weight decay 10 -4 ) and a cosine annealing schedule over at most 70 epochs, with early stopping (patience 12) on validation macro F1 and gradient clipping at a maximum norm of 1.0.

text.text: After every epoch we saved the weights, optimizer state, best validation F1, and early-stopping counter to Google Drive so training could resume after a runtime disconnect.
All deep models ran on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 in Google Colaboratory.
The M6 pipeline ran on the Colab CPU runtime.
The MiniRocket transform of all 21,375 records took 60.5 min (0.17 s per record), and LightGBM took 22.1 min (30.3 min with SMOTE).
Each model was trained once with seed 42, so the confidence intervals reflect sampling of the test set only, not run-torun training variation, which we did not measure.
Small gaps, such as M2 versus M3 (0.001) and M4 versus M1 (0.013), should be read with this in mind.
The learning rate and batch size of each deep model were set by hand and not tuned.
Training stopped through early stopping on validation macro F1 (patience 12, maximum 70 epochs), and the best-validation checkpoint was used.
We did not record the epoch at which each run stopped.
Inference was rerun from each deep model's best-validation checkpoint, with per-record class probabilities saved, and macro F1 matched the values from our initial runs to within 0.0011.
All comparisons use the same 3,182 test records.
Confidence intervals come from a patient-level paired bootstrap, in which we resampled test patients with replacement 10,000 times and scored every model on each resample.
We also ran exact McNemar tests on per-record correctness, with Holm adjustment across all 21 model pairs among M1 to M4, M5T, M6, and M6 S .
We call two models equivalent in macro F1 only if the 90% CI of their difference lies within ±0.02, and we report the 90% interval with every equivalence claim.
We set this margin before looking at results, and it is close to the half-width of a single model's 95% CI on this test set.
When the criterion is not met, we say only that no significant difference was found.

Besides macro F1, we report one-vsrest AUROC and AUPRC (per class and macro-averaged), sensitivity, specificity, and PPV at the argmax operating point, and calibration (expected calibration error with 15 bins, Brier score, and log loss).
We also report patient-level bootstrap intervals (2,000 resamples) for macro and HYP AUROC and AUPRC, including paired M6 -M5T differences.
The other per-class AUROC and AUPRC values come without intervals, and we made no correction for multiple comparisons.

text.text: Because our split is patient-disjoint but not the recommended strat_fold partition, we cannot attribute any gap with published numbers to stricter evaluation.
We compared six ECG classification approaches on 21,375 PTB-XL records using one patient-level split throughout.
Our main finding is that no model clearly outperformed MiniRocket+LightGBM on macro F1.
The ensemble selected on validation (M5, M1+M3+M4) scored 0.656, and the all-four ensemble scored 0.657.

Both were ahead of the Mamba-style and CRNN models, but neither was detectably ahead of the ResNet, the BiLSTM, or MiniRocket+LightGBM (+0.011 and +0.012 macro F1 over M6, with 95% CIs including zero).

The exploratory ensemble of M2, M3, and M4 reached 0.665 and was modestly ahead of MiniRocket+LightGBM (+0.021, 95% CI 0.002-0.040), but its members were chosen on test results, so we treat that margin as optimistic.

MiniRocket+LightGBM came close on accuracy and threshold-free metrics and had a higher HYP AUROC than both ensembles (0.871 versus 0.839 for M5 and 0.849 for M5T), although it labeled more abnormal ECGs as NORM (15.2% versus 10.0% for M5 and 12.0% for M5T).
Under our ±0.02 criterion it was also equivalent to the ResNet and BiLSTM on macro F1.
It also trains without a GPU and did not benefit from SMOTE.
The Mamba-style model scored below the CNN and BiLSTM.
Differences in HYP recall mostly reflect threshold choice, and our preprocessing, which removes amplitude information, may also limit HYP performance.
The dataset is fairly small, and the conclusions could change with a larger N .
We used only one dataset and one split.

We had no external validation, subgroup analysis, or clinically defined operating points, and we did not evaluate on the recommended strat_fold partition, so our absolute numbers cannot be compared directly with published benchmarks.
None of the models used self-supervised pretraining, which could change the ranking, and we did not test a 1D vision transformer.
We adopted the validation-based ensemble rule after first examining the test-selected ensemble, which is why we report that ensemble as exploratory.
The single-label ground truth depends on a tie-breaking rule that changes 14.6% of labels, and 23.7% of records carry more than one superclass.
Z-score normalization, the 40 Hz low-pass filter, and limblead permutation may have hurt HYP, MI, and axis-dependent classes, and we did not ablate them.
The equivalence margin was our own choice.
Each model was trained once, so our intervals do not capture training variability.
Intervals for AUROC and AUPRC cover only macro and HYP values, use 2,000 resamples, and are not corrected for multiple comparisons, and no model was calibrated.

Future work includes pretraining, evaluation on the official strat_fold partition (fold 9 for validation, fold 10 for testing) with repeated cross-validation and multiple training seeds, so that results can be compared with published benchmarks, multi-label evaluation, ablations of preprocessing and augmentation, and external clinical validation before any deployment.
